thread.title: The Rise Of Wearables For Both Consumers And Industries

author: Prableen Bajpai
title: The Rise Of Wearables For Both Consumers And Industries
text:
Fitbit (Shutterstock photo)
Gone are the days when "wearable" was used to describe comfortable clothes. It’s now a blanket term used for devices or technology connected to internet, embedded in clothes, glasses, caps, watches, or ear plugs. In other words, technology that is considered to be (obviously) "‘wearable."
Wearables are gaining wide acceptance thanks to the utility, convenience, and engagement they offer. This trend is in sync with the rise of the Internet of Things (IoT), big data, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and cloud computing.
Here’s a look at the wearables space.
The number of shipments is increasing
The shipment of wearable devices reached 115.4 million units in 2017, up 10.3% vis-à-vis 2016. IDC forecasts that the worldwide wearables market will ship 122.6 million units in 2018 and further reach 190.4 million units by 2022. A report by CCS Insight predicts the global wearables sales will reach 243 million units by 2022, growing at an average of 20% over the next five years to become a $29 billion market. While another report projects the wearables market size to be $32.42 billion by 2023, growing at a CAGR of 38.8% from 2017 to 2023.
Smartwatches, wristbands are the most well-adopted wearables
Smartwatches continue remain the most popular wearable, representing around one-third of the shipment volume and two-thirds of the markets in terms of spend due to high price tags as per IDC. This segment is expected to capture around 38% of the wearables market by 2022 with around 84.1 million shipments.
Apple, Inc. ( AAPL ) is a strong player in this segment. With the launch of its Watch Series 4 in September, Apple has introduced newer features such as LTE connectivity, fall monitor, heart rate senor, and ECG, among other features. A recent survey by Counterpoint Research reports the Apple as the most preferred smartwatch brand with more than two out of five people choosing Apple over any other brand. Samsung and Fitbit came second and third on the consumer preference list.
The rise in popularity of smartwatches does not undermine fitness trackers and wristbands which enjoy its own market share; together smartwatches, basic watches, and wristbands dominate more than 90% of the wearables market.
The launches of Versa , Charge 3, Ace, and Aria by Fitbit ( FIT ) is helping it regain its lost market share. Fitbit has recently reported its quarterly earnings, which reflected the gain in momentum.
“We saw sequential growth in both tracker and smartwatch devices,” said James Park, co-founder and CEO. “We are now the number two player in the smartwatch space in the U.S.—a category we just entered with zero share only fourteen months ago.” Fitbit sold 3.5 million wearable devices driven by the growing mix of smartwatches.
Xiaomi, Huawei and Garmin are some other popular brands which together with Apple and Fitbit hold more than 50% of the global wearables market share. While wrist-worn devices dominate wearables market, eyewear, hearables and clothing are seeing increased usage and adoption, although they are under 10% of the overall market.
While these products are popular with consumers, wearable devices are capable of far more scalable use in diverse industries along with other advanced technologies
Wearables have great utility that lends themselves well to certain industries such as healthcare, manufacturing, mining, transportation and logistics.
A range of wearable such as caps, cameras, head-mounted displays have the potential to enhance security in logistics and transportation and even in high-risk industries such as mining. Such devices can track the activity of the driver or mine worker to connect and track patterns and thus alert and reduce number of fatigue-related accidents, among other benefits.
Global manufacturers are adopting ‘mixed reality’ to enhance productivity, quality, and safety in operations. BAE Systems and PTC, Honeywell, Mercedes Benz are experimenting with mixed reality using Microsoft’s ( MSFT ) HoloLens.
With the objective to improve accuracy and reduce the complexity of aircraft assembly, Accenture and Airbus used Vuzix ( VUZI ) industrial-grade smart glasses for cabin seat marking process in 2016 and the results were remarkable: the overall productivity of the marking process improved 500%, error rate reduced to zero, while accelerating the marking operation significantly. The technology has been industrialized for Airbus 330 long range aircraft seat marking and installation since then; other projects are underway.
While smartwatches and wristbands get all the attention, the scope for wearables in core operations across industries to enhance efficiency and security is immense.
